nameStory: Tree Jelly gets its name from its remarkable texture when wet – it becomes soft, rubbery, and translucent like gelatin! When dry, this lichen transforms into a completely different-looking crusty or papery mass, but add some rain or morning dew and it plumps back up into its jelly-like form. It's like nature's own shape-shifting magic trick happening right on tree bark.
description: Tree Jelly is a fascinating foliose lichen that dramatically changes appearance with moisture. When wet, it forms dark olive-green to blackish, translucent, jelly-like lobes that feel rubbery to the touch. When dry, it shrinks into dark, brittle, almost unrecognizable crusty patches. Individual colonies typically grow 1-3 inches across, forming irregular rosettes or overlapping patches on tree bark.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose (leafy) lichen with broad, rounded lobes that overlap like shingles when wet, becoming wrinkled and contracted when dry

idTips.label: Texture When Wet
idTips.description: Soft, rubbery, and jelly-like – you can gently press it and feel it give like gelatin; translucent enough to see through in places

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to brownish-black when wet and plump; becomes much darker, almost black and brittle when completely dry

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on tree bark, especially favoring smooth-barked deciduous trees like maples, birches, and sometimes oaks

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth and glossy when wet with no powdery coating; may have tiny wrinkles or ridges but feels uniformly soft throughout

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies range from thumbnail-size to about 3 inches across; lobes are typically 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide

habitat: Tree Jelly grows on the bark of deciduous trees in moist, shaded environments throughout New England's forests. Look for it in mature mixed woods, especially near streams, wetlands, or north-facing slopes where humidity stays higher. It particularly favors smooth-barked trees like sugar maple, paper birch, and American beech at elevations from sea level to mid-mountain slopes.

seasonality.spring: Most visible during wet spring weather when it plumps up into its characteristic jelly-like form. Morning dew and spring rains bring out the best olive-green coloration.
seasonality.summer: Often dried and contracted during hot, dry periods, appearing as dark crusty patches. Best observed after summer thunderstorms when it quickly rehydrates.
seasonality.fall: Frequent fall rains keep it hydrated and visible in its gelatinous form. The darker fall lighting makes the translucent quality especially noticeable.
seasonality.winter: Alternates between wet jelly-like state during thaws and brittle dry patches during cold, dry periods. Snow melt can dramatically transform its appearance within hours.

funFact: Tree Jelly can lose up to 95% of its water content and appear completely dead, then fully rehydrate and return to active photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet – a superpower that lets it survive in places where most plants would perish from repeated drying cycles!
confusionNotes: When dry, Tree Jelly looks completely different and might be mistaken for a crusty black fungal growth or even lichens in different families entirely. The key memory trick: if you find a mysterious dark crusty patch on tree bark after dry weather, sprinkle some water on it – if it's Tree Jelly, you'll see it start to plump up and turn olive-green within minutes!
contextualKnowledge: Tree Jelly belongs to a special group called 'cyanolichens' because they partner with cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) instead of regular green algae. This partnership gives them their unique jelly-like texture and their ability to fix nitrogen from the air, actually helping to fertilize the forest ecosystem around them.
compareHints: Since Tree Jelly is the only Collema species commonly found in New England, compare it with other gelatinous lichens like Nostoc (which forms blob-like masses on soil rather than growing on bark) or various Leptogium species (which tend to be thinner, more papery, and often have a different color when wet). Tree Jelly's thick, truly jelly-like texture when wet and its preference for deciduous tree bark help distinguish it from these relatives.
